misreadings.inContext: Each verse is true, and the sequence is a useful evangelistic tool. But in context, 3:23 explains why Jew and Gentile stand on level ground (3:22, 3:29); 6:23 is addressed to believers about which master they serve; 10:9-10 answers Israel's story in Deut 30 and the confession 'Jesus is Lord' would sound in Rome like a challenge to 'Caesar is Lord'. Scholars from Wright to Scot McKnight (*The King Jesus Gospel*, 2011) argue that reducing the gospel to a personal plan of salvation leaves out Jesus as Israel's Messiah and Lord, and the creation of one people.
misreadings.defence: Defenders, including many evangelical pastors and scholars like Schreiner, reply that the Romans Road accurately reflects Paul's own logic (sin, grace, faith) and that evangelism needs simple summaries. They agree the full gospel also includes resurrection, lordship and church, and that the Road is a door into Romans, not a replacement for it.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Using the verses is not wrong; using them as the whole of Romans can make the gospel only about escaping punishment, rather than also about belonging to a Lord and his people.

perspectives.name: Lutheran and Reformed (traditional Protestant)
perspectives.who: Martin Luther, John Calvin; modern: Douglas Moo, Thomas Schreiner, Stephen Westerholm, Simon Gathercole, D. A. Carson, John Piper
perspectives.summary: Romans answers the universal human problem: all are guilty before a holy God, and none can earn favour. God justifies the ungodly by grace through faith alone, on the basis of Christ's atoning death, crediting righteousness to believers. Law and gospel are sharply distinguished: the Law exposes sin; the gospel gives what the Law demands.
perspectives.strengths: Takes seriously Paul's language of guilt, wrath, gift and 'the ungodly' (Rom 4:5); gives deep personal assurance; has carefully answered New Perspective claims with studies of Second Temple Judaism.
perspectives.critiques: Critics say it can read Paul through Luther's late-medieval struggles and caricature Judaism as legalism, and can neglect Jew-Gentile unity, Israel's story and Rom 9-16. Defenders reply that the best Reformed scholars now avoid the caricature and that the individual and social belong together.

perspectives.name: New Perspective on Paul
perspectives.who: E. P. Sanders (groundwork), James D. G. Dunn (named it, 1983), N. T. Wright
perspectives.summary: Judaism was a religion of grace and covenant, not merit-earning. Paul's critique of 'works of the law' targets Torah used as a boundary marker that excluded Gentiles. Justification is God's declaration of who belongs to the covenant people, marked by faith in Jesus, so Jews and Gentiles eat together.
perspectives.strengths: Corrects anti-Jewish caricatures; explains why Romans spends so long on Abraham, Israel and food laws; makes the social shape of the gospel central.
perspectives.critiques: Critics (Westerholm, Gathercole, Carson) say it underplays Paul's universal language about human sin and works, overstates uniformity in Judaism, and risks making justification mainly about the church. Many on both sides now accept parts of each other's insights.

perspectives.name: Paul within Judaism
perspectives.who: Krister Stendahl (forerunner), Mark Nanos, Pamela Eisenbaum, Paula Fredriksen, Magnus Zetterholm, Matthew Thiessen
perspectives.summary: Paul never left Judaism. He remained a Torah-observant Jew and wrote Romans to Gentile believers, telling them not to become Jews but to join Israel's God as Gentiles. His criticisms of the Law concern Gentiles taking it on, not Jews keeping it.
perspectives.strengths: Takes Paul's Jewishness and Rom 11 with full seriousness; notes that the letter's explicit audience is Gentile (Rom 1:13; 11:13); combats Christian anti-Judaism.
perspectives.critiques: Critics say it struggles with texts where Paul seems to address Jews (Rom 2:17) or relativise the Law for all (Rom 7:4-6; 14:14), and with Paul's insistence that Jews too need the Messiah (Rom 10:1-4). Some versions suggest a 'two covenant' view that most interpreters think Rom 10-11 excludes.

perspectives.name: Apocalyptic Paul
perspectives.who: Ernst Käsemann, J. Louis Martyn (mainly on Galatians), Beverly Gaventa, Douglas Campbell
perspectives.summary: Romans is about God's invasive rescue of a world held captive by Sin and Death as powers. God's righteousness is his liberating, world-changing action in Christ. Human beings are not mainly lawbreakers needing a verdict but captives needing deliverance.
perspectives.strengths: Explains Paul's language of Sin as a ruling power (Rom 5-7), creation's groaning (Rom 8) and the cosmic scope of salvation; stresses God's initiative.
perspectives.critiques: Critics say it can downplay Israel's story and covenant continuity, and human responsibility. Campbell's reading of Rom 1-4 as Paul quoting an opponent is widely judged unconvincing even by sympathetic scholars.

perspectives.name: Paul and the Gift (Barclay)
perspectives.who: John M. G. Barclay (*Paul and the Gift*, 2015; *Paul and the Power of Grace*, 2020)
perspectives.summary: In the ancient world 'grace' could be 'perfected' (emphasised) in different ways: its size, its priority, its being given to the unworthy, its effect, or its not expecting a return. Paul's distinctive emphasis is grace given without regard to worth (incongruous grace), which undermines all prior status, Jewish or Gentile, and forms new communities. But it is not 'non-circular': it expects grateful, transformed lives.
perspectives.strengths: Bridges the Old and New Perspectives: grace is truly free and also social. Explains why Jewish texts could all speak of grace yet differ from Paul.
perspectives.critiques: Some Reformed readers want a clearer place for imputation and forensic justification; some New Perspective readers think it still centres too much on grace as a theme. Widely praised as one of the most important recent books on Paul.

perspectives.name: Eastern Orthodox
perspectives.who: John Chrysostom's *Homilies on Romans* (late 4th century), Theodoret; modern Orthodox writers
perspectives.summary: Romans is read as the story of God healing humanity from death and corruption through union with Christ (theosis, sharing in God's life). Rom 5:12 is read as Adam passing on death and mortality, not inherited guilt. Faith and works are not set against each other; salvation is a lifelong participation in Christ through baptism and the Spirit.
perspectives.strengths: Reads Rom 6 and 8 (union, Spirit, adoption, glory) as central; keeps a long patristic memory, including Greek-speaking readers of Paul's own language.
perspectives.critiques: Protestant critics say it underplays the legal language of justification and Paul's 'apart from works'. Orthodox reply that the Western legal frame is itself one emphasis that should not swallow participation.

keyTerms.usual: The message of how to be saved and go to heaven.
keyTerms.inContext: In the Greek Old Testament and Isaiah, 'good news' announces that God reigns and is bringing his people home (Isa 52:7). In Roman inscriptions it announced imperial births and victories. Paul's gospel is about God's Son, descended from David and declared Son of God by resurrection: a royal announcement.

keyTerms.usual: Moral perfection; to justify is to declare a sinner legally innocent.
keyTerms.inContext: The same Greek root covers 'righteousness', 'justice' and 'justification'. It translates Hebrew tsedaqah: rightness within a relationship, including God's faithful saving action. To be 'justified' is to be declared in the right, in God's court and within his people.

keyTerms.usual: Believing certain facts, or inner trust as opposed to doing.
keyTerms.inContext: Trust, faithfulness and loyalty in a relationship. Paul speaks of the 'obedience of faith'. Abraham's faith is trusting God's promise against the evidence. Whether it means 'faithfulness' in pistis Christou is debated.

keyTerms.usual: Unearned favour, opposed to any human response.
keyTerms.inContext: A gift or benefaction in a culture of patronage, which created a bond and expected gratitude. Paul stresses grace given to the unworthy and ungodly, which still produces a response of grateful service.

Deeds the Torah requires, often focused in debate on practices that set Jews apart (circumcision, food, Sabbath). A similar Hebrew phrase appears in a Dead Sea Scroll (4QMMT). Its exact scope is a central scholarly debate.

keyTerms.usual: God's moral rules in general, or legalism.
keyTerms.inContext: Usually the Torah of Moses, the covenant gift given to Israel at Sinai. Paul sometimes plays on nomos as 'principle' or 'rule' (Rom 7:21-23; 8:2).

keyTerms.usual: A sacrifice that turns away God's anger.
keyTerms.inContext: In the Greek Old Testament the word names the 'mercy seat', the lid of the ark where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. Translations differ between 'propitiation' (turning away wrath), 'expiation' (wiping out sin) and 'mercy seat'; many scholars think Paul includes the Day of Atonement imagery.

keyTerms.usual: The body, or sinful physical desires.
keyTerms.inContext: Human existence in its weakness and mortality, and, for Paul, life organised apart from God's Spirit. It can also mean ethnic descent ('according to the flesh', Rom 9:3-5).

keyTerms.usual: A private inner experience of God.
keyTerms.inContext: God's own presence, promised by the prophets for the age of return (Ezek 36-37), now given to Jews and Gentiles, writing the Law on hearts, adopting them as children and raising the dead.

keyTerms.usual: A warm picture of being loved by God.
keyTerms.inContext: A Roman legal act that transferred a person, often an adult, into a new family with full inheritance rights and cancelled old debts. It also echoes Israel as God's 'son' (Exod 4:22; Rom 9:4).
In the Greek Old Testament kyrios stands for God's name, YHWH; in Rome it was used of the emperor. 'Jesus is Lord' (Rom 10:9) applies Joel 2:32 to Jesus and stakes a rival claim to Caesar's.

In Jewish apocalyptic writing (as in Daniel), a hidden plan of God now revealed. In Romans it is Israel's partial hardening until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and the gospel kept secret for ages and now disclosed.

Prophetic word for the faithful part of Israel through whom God keeps his promise to the whole (Elijah's 7,000; Isaiah's remnant). Paul sees Jewish believers like himself as the remnant chosen by grace.
